vignette:
He is a 50-year-old African man who works as a plumber and has been married for many years. Before the assault, he describes himself as steady and practical, the kind of man who takes pride in fixing what is broken and coming home with enough energy to sit with his wife in the evening and talk about the day. His work is physical and familiar to him; pipes, leaks, and clogged drains make sense in a way people sometimes do not. He has spent most of his adult life moving between job sites, carrying tools, solving problems, and being known as someone who can be counted on.

The assault happens unexpectedly. He is out doing an ordinary errand when a confrontation turns violent. He does not talk about every detail in the same way each time, but the parts he returns to are consistent: the shock of being cornered, the sense that things happen too fast for him to think, the helplessness of realizing that his body is reacting before his mind can make sense of what is unfolding. He remembers the sound of raised voices, the sudden impact, and then a fierce, disorganizing fear that leaves him feeling both exposed and humiliated. In the days afterward, he keeps replaying the event in fragments, trying to identify the moment when it might have turned out differently. He says that what bothers him most is not only the injury or the fear, but the feeling that he was taken by surprise and could not protect himself.

After the assault, he does not return to his usual rhythm. He starts sleeping lightly, waking at the smallest sound, and lying awake with his mind moving back to the event. Nights become the hardest part of the day. He often sits up in bed with his heart racing, listening to the house settle, scanning for danger even though he knows, rationally, that he is home and safe. He avoids certain streets and will change his route if he thinks he might pass the place where it happened. When he is out in public, he keeps his eyes moving and positions himself so he can see who is behind him. He notices men standing too close in a line or speaking loudly nearby and feels his muscles tighten before he can stop it.

At work, the change is obvious to him and to others. Plumbing has always required focus, but now he finds himself distracted by sudden memories and jolted by unexpected noises like a hammer dropping or a colleague calling his name. He is careful in a new way, almost rigidly so, checking and rechecking his tools, the van, the locks on doors, and the spaces around him. He says he cannot afford mistakes, but underneath that is a persistent feeling that something bad could happen again at any moment. On some days he struggles to start the workday at all; he stands over a sink or crouches by a pipe and feels as though his mind has drifted somewhere else. He can complete the job, but it takes more effort and leaves him exhausted.

He becomes more irritable with the people closest to him. His wife notices that he snaps more quickly, withdraws into silence, and seems far less patient than before. He does not want to be touched unexpectedly, even by her, and he feels ashamed when he flinches. He is not comfortable talking about the assault, and when others ask how he is doing, he often says he is fine because he does not have the words for the mixture of anger, fear, and embarrassment he carries. Inside, he feels changed in a way that is hard to explain. He no longer trusts his surroundings in the same way, and he is unsettled by the fact that ordinary things—a car backfiring, footsteps behind him, a crowded room—can send a jolt through him as if the assault were happening again.

As the months pass, he tries to push himself to keep going. He continues working, caring for his home, and maintaining the responsibilities that matter to him, but he does so with a constant effort that others do not always see. He measures his days by what he can manage and what he must avoid. He still wants to be the dependable man he has always been, yet he feels that part of him remains stuck in the moment of the assault, alert and braced for danger, even when nothing is there.
